demos.title: From chat to a reviewed change
demos.scenario: The inventory service needs a health check.
demos.payoff: A reviewed pull request with passing CI
demos.next: What could your team hand off next?
demos.intro: Our inventory service has no health check. A developer wants to add one, with a test and updated documentation. They will ask through Claude Code. Orka will run the work on the team's infrastructure and keep the records. Let's follow that request all the way to a reviewed pull request.

chapters.title: Start with the missing endpoint
chapters.cue: A small change with a result we can check
chapters.text: Here is the service's current API. It can list, create, and retrieve inventory items. There is no health endpoint yet. That gives us a concrete change to ask for and a clear result to check at the end.

chapters.title: Meet the team Orka can run
chapters.cue: Agent = a configured worker for a particular role
chapters.text: The platform team has already installed Orka. A Provider is its connection to a model service. An Agent is a configured worker, with a model, a way to run, and permissions. Here we have a coding agent and a separate reviewer. A Task is Orka's record of one piece of work assigned to an agent.

chapters.title: Connect with a developer identity
chapters.cue: The developer authenticates to Orka
chapters.text: The developer connects to Orka with a Kubernetes service account token. Think of this as their identity for this installation. It is separate from the model provider's key. The status command confirms that Orka is ready and the team's agents are available.

chapters.marker: Point Claude Code at the cluster
chapters.title: Use the familiar chat client
chapters.cue: Claude Code sends its requests to Orka
chapters.text: Claude Code can use Orka's compatible endpoint. We set the server address and the developer's token, then list the models available to that identity. The developer keeps their familiar client, while the platform team manages the model connection in the cluster.

chapters.title: Ask for the change
chapters.cue: Describe the outcome, including tests and documentation
chapters.text: The request asks for a health endpoint, a unit test, documentation, and a pull request. We send it as an ordinary chat prompt. Orka's coordinator can turn that conversation into work for the configured agents, then bring their results back to the developer.

chapters.marker: Orka turns the conversation into Tasks
chapters.title: Follow the work as it happens
chapters.cue: Task records show implementation, checks, and review
chapters.text: Each row is a real Task. The coding agents implement the change, other tasks run checks, and the reviewer inspects the result. Waiting time is compressed here. One validation attempt fails with an older Go image, and later checks succeed. Orka keeps those attempts visible, so we can see how the work reached its result.

chapters.title: Inspect the execution and publication
chapters.cue: The publication receipt records what reached the remote
chapters.text: A Task keeps execution events as well as its final answer. We can read what the coder did and inspect the publication receipt. Orka's Publisher is a separate component that publishes the changed files. Verified Exact means the published content matched the content Orka checked.

chapters.title: Check the delivered result
chapters.cue: Real pull request, changed files, and CI result
chapters.text: Now we check the result outside the agent's answer. GitHub shows the health endpoint pull request, a passing test check, and the three changed files. The developer's chat request has become a change the team can review. The pull request remains open for the team to decide what happens next.

demos.outro: One request reached implementation, checks, review, and a real pull request. Orka kept the work records along the way. What would you hand off to your own agent team? Visit the Orka documentation at the address on screen for more examples and the getting started guide.

demos.title: A workspace that can wait
demos.scenario: Add a health check today. Pick up the work later.
demos.payoff: The worker stops. The files survive.
demos.next: What work would you return to tomorrow?
demos.intro: A developer asks an agent to add a health check to the inventory service. Later, they want to return and inspect the same files. Keeping an idle agent running wastes compute. Orka can stop its worker while keeping the workspace data. Let's see what survives between the two requests.

chapters.title: Choose how the workspace waits
chapters.cue: Session = related requests that share this workspace
chapters.text: A Session groups related requests. In this setup, those requests share one workspace. Agent Sandbox is the component that hosts the worker and its disk. A workspace class is the platform team's saved choice of host and lifecycle. This class says to suspend when work finishes. Suspension stops the worker and keeps its disk for later.

chapters.title: Give the agent a place to work
chapters.cue: Task = one request, with a recorded outcome
chapters.text: We create a Task naming the Session, the workspace class, and the repository. Orka starts a worker and attaches a disk. The agent adds the health endpoint and its test. Orka's separate Publisher publishes the changed files. In this run the worker has no Go toolchain, so the pull request's CI runs the tests.

chapters.title: Stop the idle worker
chapters.cue: No worker Pod; the stored files remain
chapters.text: The task has finished, so the workspace follows its suspend policy. Watch the worker Pod disappear while the disk remains. A Pod is the running worker here. With no Pod, this workspace uses no worker compute while it waits. The disk still exists and still has a storage cost.

chapters.marker: A follow-up in the same Session
chapters.title: Return to the same files
chapters.cue: The follow-up uses the original Session
chapters.text: The next Task names the same Session and asks to inspect the files already there. Orka starts the worker again using the kept disk. The result shows the health endpoint and test from the first request. Delivery says No Change because this follow-up only read the workspace and had nothing new to publish.

chapters.title: Finish the workspace lifecycle
chapters.cue: Workspace cleanup leaves the work records and pull request
chapters.text: When the team is finished, deleting this workspace removes its Sandbox and disk according to the configured policy. We check that those resources are gone. The pull request remains available. The working environment has a lifecycle of its own, separate from the recorded work and its published result.

demos.outro: Two requests used one set of files, with the worker stopped in between. The platform team chose the lifecycle once, and the developer used it by name. What work would you want to return to tomorrow? Explore workspace options and get started at the Orka documentation address on screen.

demos.title: Save the work. Resume somewhere new.
demos.scenario: An audit must survive a pause and a deleted workspace.
demos.payoff: The audit returns from a saved checkpoint
demos.next: What work needs a reliable handoff?
demos.intro: The security team is auditing the inventory service. One person starts the work, and a colleague will pick it up later. They also want a saved copy that survives deletion of the original workspace. Orka can manage that lifecycle and keep the records. We will follow the audit files through both handoffs.

chapters.title: Meet the workspace host
chapters.cue: Actor = an isolated environment hosted by a worker
chapters.text: Agent Substrate is the workspace host in this example. It keeps a shared pool of workers ready. An Actor is the isolated environment where one agent runs, using gVisor for isolation. Orka's workspace class says when to start and suspend it. This demo preserves files. A later request starts a fresh process with those files.

chapters.title: Write the audit
chapters.cue: A Task records the work; a Session connects follow-ups
chapters.text: A Task is one request to Orka. This one opens a Session, which groups related requests, and asks the agent to write an audit file. An Actor starts on a free worker. The response lists the input validation issues the agent found, and the publication receipt identifies the branch containing its audit.

chapters.title: Keep the files and release the worker
chapters.cue: The Actor is gone; all shared workers are available
chapters.text: After the task finishes, Orka saves the Actor's data and removes that Actor. The worker that hosted it is replaced, leaving the pool ready for other work. We see a suspended workspace, no Actors, and free workers. The shared worker pool and saved storage still exist. The audit is no longer occupying an Actor.

chapters.marker: A follow-up in the same Session
chapters.title: Resume in a fresh Actor
chapters.cue: A new Actor reads the existing audit file
chapters.text: A colleague's follow-up uses the same Session. The Actor name changes because Orka starts a fresh environment from the saved data. The result contains the original audit file and its findings. The handoff kept the working files without needing the original agent process to remain alive.

chapters.title: Keep an independent save point
chapters.cue: Checkpoint = a saved copy of the workspace data
chapters.text: A checkpoint is a saved copy of the workspace's data with its own record. We create one and wait until it is ready. The digest is a fingerprint of that saved data. The checkpoint can be named by a later task even after the original workspace is removed.

chapters.marker: Delete the original, restore the copy
chapters.title: Restore after deleting the source
chapters.cue: A new Task restores the saved checkpoint
chapters.text: We delete the original workspace and confirm it is gone. Then a new Task, outside the old Session, names the checkpoint and its fingerprint. The restored workspace contains the same audit. Its files can be published again, and the new Task gets its own publication receipt.

chapters.title: Check the resources left behind
chapters.cue: No active Actors remain after the demonstration
chapters.text: The final check shows no active Actors and a worker pool ready for more tasks. We also remove the demo's checkpoint once the restore is verified. That makes the retained data an explicit choice the team can manage.

demos.outro: The audit survived a pause, a fresh agent environment, and deletion of its original workspace. Orka connected the requests and tracked the saved data. Which handoff would you make more reliable? Visit the Orka documentation at the address on screen to explore workspaces and get started.

demos.title: From a checked finding to a fix
demos.scenario: A legacy service needs a security review people can act on.
demos.payoff: A selected finding becomes a real pull request
demos.next: Which repository would you review first?
demos.intro: A security team wants to review an old service and help engineers act on the results. For this example, we use a public test application with known vulnerabilities. Orka will coordinate the scan and keep its findings. A person will choose one finding to fix, then inspect the resulting pull request.

chapters.title: Tell Orka what to review
chapters.cue: RepositoryScan = the saved instructions for scanning a repository
chapters.text: A Repository Scan records which repository to inspect and which agents should analyze and patch it. An agent is a configured worker with a model and permissions. This configuration also names the credential references used for repository operations. Registering it starts the first scan. The team can return to its results through the same record.

chapters.title: Watch the review take shape
chapters.cue: Task records show the scan's progress
chapters.text: Orka first asks for a threat model, a short description of the application and where an attacker might affect it. It then assigns parts of the code to review tasks. A Task is Orka's record of one piece of work. These rows show the actual progress, with quiet waiting compressed. The scan also tries to validate likely findings.

chapters.title: Read the evidence for one finding
chapters.cue: Validated and unvalidated findings remain distinct
chapters.text: The results distinguish validated findings from findings that still need checking. We inspect a validated archive extraction issue. A crafted archive could write files outside the intended directory. The finding identifies the source file, location, and behavior, giving the team something specific to investigate. This evidence supports the selected finding. It does not prove the whole application is secure.

chapters.marker: A person decides to fix it
chapters.title: Choose a finding and inspect the fix
chapters.cue: The person selects the work; the pull request remains reviewable
chapters.text: The presenter selects that finding for a patch. Orka gives it to the coding agent, tracks the task, and publishes the result through its Publisher component. We then check GitHub itself. The pull request is open and lists the changed files. The team can review the proposed fix using its normal process.

demos.outro: The scan produced a checked finding, a person selected it, and Orka delivered a pull request for review. The evidence and the fix stay connected. Which repository would you start with? Visit the Orka documentation at the address on screen for more examples and the getting started guide.

demos.title: One URL. Separate teams.
demos.scenario: Payments and inventory need different models and separate work.
demos.payoff: The caller's identity selects the team
demos.next: How would you organize your agent teams?
demos.intro: Payments and inventory both want to use AI agents. Each team needs its own model configuration and work records, but developers want one familiar server address. In this setup, each team has its own Orka installation. A small router uses the caller's identity to send requests to the right team.

chapters.title: Give each team its own installation
chapters.cue: Namespace = a named area for one team's resources
chapters.text: Each team has a separate Kubernetes namespace, a named area containing its own Orka resources. Its Provider is the connection to its chosen model service. Payments uses one model, inventory another. The router's configuration maps each team to its installation. The router forwards requests. Each team's Orka performs the work.

chapters.title: Connect two people to the same address
chapters.cue: Same endpoint; different authenticated identities
chapters.text: Alice belongs to payments and Bob belongs to inventory. Both use the same server address. Their service account tokens identify their teams. When we ask which models are available, the answers differ. Each person sees the models configured by their own team's installation.

chapters.title: See where the requests become work
chapters.cue: Task = the record of work inside the selected team
chapters.text: Both developers now ask for the same simple container task. A Task is Orka's record of a piece of work. The answers come back through the shared endpoint, and the task lists show where the work ran. Payments tasks are in payments. Inventory tasks are in inventory.

chapters.title: Try the wrong team's resources
chapters.cue: Both the router path and direct installation enforce identity
chapters.text: Bob tries to name the payments Provider. His request still reaches inventory, where that Provider does not exist. Then he contacts the payments installation directly and asks to list its tasks. That request receives a forbidden response. The team installation checks identity too, so the boundary does not depend only on the shared router.

chapters.title: Check the separate work records
chapters.cue: One client address, with work kept in each team's installation
chapters.text: The final list shows completed tasks under both team namespaces. Developers used one address while the platform kept each team's configuration and records separate. The requests we tested stayed within the caller's team, and the cross-team attempts were refused.

demos.outro: One endpoint can serve separate teams without putting their work in the same installation. Each team keeps control of its configured models and task records. How would you organize your agent teams? Explore the options and the getting started guide at the Orka documentation address on screen.

demos.title: The order desk asks Orka for help
demos.scenario: A customer wants 24 filters. Only 18 are available today.
demos.payoff: A saved reply the order desk can retrieve again
demos.next: Which application could use your agents?
demos.intro: A customer wants twenty four replacement filters today. We have eighteen, and the next delivery arrives tomorrow. The order desk needs advice from the inventory team's agent. That agent runs in Orka. We will ask it from another application, retry the request, and see whether the answer remains available.

chapters.title: Start with the customer's situation
chapters.cue: 24 requested; 18 available; next delivery tomorrow
chapters.text: These are the facts the order desk has. The request asks for a recommendation and a short customer reply. It also says not to place an order or promise an exact delivery time. The terminal is standing in for the order-desk application.

chapters.title: Discover what the agent can do
chapters.cue: Agent Card = a description of an agent and how to contact it
chapters.text: The application reads an Agent Card. This describes the agent's purpose and the work it supports. Here, the advertised skill is recommending a customer reply. A two A is the common message format the application and Orka use to communicate, so the application can ask for work through a standard interface.

chapters.title: Submit the request and keep its reference
chapters.cue: Task = Orka's record of one piece of work
chapters.text: We send the facts with a stable request identifier and ask for an immediate acknowledgement. The response gives us a reference for checking progress. In Orka, a Task is the record of one piece of work. We can inspect the matching Task without keeping the application's original connection open.

chapters.title: Read the real answer
chapters.cue: The application answer matches Orka's saved result
chapters.text: The completed answer offers eighteen filters today and explains that six remain for the next delivery. We retrieve it through the application client, then read Orka's stored result. They match. The response is based on the quantities and timing supplied in the request.

chapters.title: Retry the same request
chapters.cue: Same request ID and content return the original Task
chapters.text: Applications retry when they are unsure a request arrived. We repeat the same request identifier, conversation, and text. The returned reference is the same, and the recorded evidence finds just one matching Task with the same identity. This retry created no extra piece of work.

chapters.title: Continue the conversation
chapters.cue: Session = the conversation shared by related Tasks
chapters.text: Now we ask for a two-sentence customer reply. This is new work, so it gets a new request identifier. The conversation identifier stays the same. Orka calls that shared conversation a Session. The saved records show two distinct Tasks in one Session, and the follow-up uses the earlier facts.

chapters.title: Retrieve the answer after replacement
chapters.cue: The adapter handles messages; Orka retains the work records
chapters.text: The adapter translates the application's messages. Both tasks have finished before we replace it. Once its replacement is ready, we retrieve the answer again. The evidence shows the same saved reply and no new Tasks. This demonstrates continued access to completed results after replacing the adapter. It does not test interrupting an agent while it is working.

demos.outro: The order desk got a usable reply, retried safely, and continued the conversation. It could still read the answer after the message adapter was replaced. Which application could use your agents this way? Visit the Orka documentation at the address on screen to explore more and get started.

demos.title: Check stock. Keep purchasing closed.
demos.scenario: The assistant needs supplier information, without buying anything.
demos.next: Which actions should your platform allow?
demos.intro: The inventory team needs twenty more replacement filters. Its supplier can check stock and accept orders. Our assistant should gather information, but purchasing is not enabled. Orka will run the requests through a configured gateway. We will compare the assistant's tool events with the supplier's own receipts.

chapters.title: Ask for information first
chapters.cue: The supplier simulator starts with zero orders
chapters.text: The request asks whether twenty filters are available. Our supplier is a small HTTP service with synthetic stock and real request receipts. Its order count starts at zero. That gives us a baseline for checking whether anything gets purchased during this run.

chapters.marker: 2. How the assistant reaches the supplier
chapters.title: Define the action the model can request
chapters.cue: Tool = a named action the model can ask Orka to carry out
chapters.text: A Tool is a named action the model can ask Orka to carry out. This Tool describes an HTTP stock lookup. Its outbound policy tells Orka to send the request through a gateway. Both stock lookup and ordering are available for the model to request here, which lets us test the gateway's independent restriction.

chapters.title: Read the route and credential reference
chapters.cue: The gateway permits the stock route and supplies its credential
chapters.text: A gateway sits between Orka and the supplier. A route defines which request it can forward. This route permits the stock lookup. The credential reference points to a Kubernetes Secret, where the platform keeps the supplier credential. The gateway supplies that credential. The Tool definition does not contain it.

chapters.title: Run the allowed lookup
chapters.cue: Task = the work record, including tool events and the result
chapters.text: A Task is Orka's record of one piece of work. We create a lookup Task and see its tool call start and complete. The assistant reports thirty two filters available, enough to cover the twenty needed. Next, we check the service's record of that lookup.

chapters.title: Check what reached the supplier
chapters.cue: The receipt confirms the request and accepted credential
chapters.text: The supplier receipt shows the stock endpoint, the requested item, and thirty two available units. It also says the credential was accepted. This connects the assistant's answer to an authenticated request that actually reached the supplier service.

chapters.marker: 6. Ask it to place an order
chapters.title: Attempt the closed operation
chapters.cue: The gateway refuses the order because no route matches
chapters.text: We explicitly ask the assistant to use its order Tool. The call reaches the gateway, which returns HTTP four oh four because no order route is configured. Orka records the failed call, and the assistant reports that failure. Being able to request an action did not give the model permission to complete it.

chapters.title: Compare both sides of the request
chapters.cue: Allowed lookup; no order request received by the supplier
chapters.text: The summary is calculated from this run's records. The stock lookup reached the supplier with an accepted credential. The gateway refused the order, the supplier received zero order requests, and it created zero orders. These checks apply to the two configured Tools shown in this example.

demos.outro: The assistant gathered useful stock information while purchasing stayed closed. The gateway controlled the route and supplied the supplier credential. Which actions should your platform allow? Visit the Orka documentation at the address on screen to explore tool access and follow the getting started guide.

demos.title: A procedure the next agent can use
demos.scenario: Keep a return procedure, with a person deciding what is shared.
demos.payoff: A fresh agent uses the reviewed procedure
demos.next: Which team knowledge is worth keeping?
demos.intro: An assistant has read a warehouse return procedure. Returned filters go to Dock Three with a particular return label. The next person will need those instructions too. Orka lets an agent propose useful information to keep, while a person decides whether to publish it as shared knowledge. Let's follow that process.

chapters.title: Start with the source note
chapters.cue: Memory = saved project information supplied to future work
chapters.text: The note names Dock Three and the exact return label shown here. In this demo, memory means saved project information that Orka supplies to future tasks. We begin with no shared notes. The first assistant has the procedure only because its task receives this source note.

chapters.title: Let the agent suggest what to keep
chapters.cue: remember creates a proposal for review
chapters.text: A Task is the record of one piece of work. We ask an assistant to identify the reusable procedure and propose it. Its remember tool call starts and completes. Despite the tool's name, this step creates a proposal for review. It does not immediately create shared memory.

chapters.title: Read the proposal and its source
chapters.cue: The proposal records its text, originating Task, and status
chapters.text: We list proposals from this Task and open the matching record. It contains the procedure, the Task it came from, and a pending status. A reviewer can check the exact text against the original note before deciding what should become available to future work.

chapters.title: Try the question before publication
chapters.cue: No shared Session; zero reader tool calls
chapters.text: A different reader gets only the question in a fresh Task. It shares no Session, so it receives no earlier conversation. We instruct it to use only reviewed notes already supplied and to call no tools. It says the procedure is unavailable. The event record confirms zero tool calls. We verify that behavior rather than claiming its tools were disabled.

chapters.title: Record the human decision
chapters.cue: Accepted proposal; still zero shared notes
chapters.text: The presenter checks the proposal against the source and accepts it. The record now identifies the review decision and reviewer. But the shared note count is still zero, and there is no applied memory identifier. Accepting a proposal records the decision. Publishing the note is a separate action.

chapters.title: Publish the reviewed note
chapters.cue: Apply creates shared memory linked to the proposal
chapters.text: Now we apply the accepted proposal. Orka creates the shared memory, and the list shows the procedure with a reference to its source proposal. That link lets the team connect the saved knowledge back to the review and the work that produced it.

chapters.title: Ask a new reader the same question
chapters.cue: Exact dock and label recalled with zero tool calls
chapters.text: We start another fresh Task with the same reader and question. We do not attach the source note or the earlier conversation. This time the answer contains Dock Three and the exact return label. Again, the recorded tool count is zero. The reader used the reviewed memory Orka supplied when the task started.

chapters.title: Follow the saved links
chapters.cue: Original Task → proposal → review → memory → later Task
chapters.text: These identifiers come from the saved records. Together they connect the original Task, proposal, review decision, applied memory, and later answer. Both readers made zero tool calls. The before and after difference is the reviewed note becoming available to the new task.

demos.outro: One agent proposed a useful procedure. A person reviewed and applied it. A later agent could use it, with a record linking the knowledge to its source. Which team knowledge is worth keeping? Explore reviewed memory and get started at the Orka documentation address on screen.

demos.title: Fibey investigates. A person approves.
demos.scenario: A pressure reading changed after maintenance. Inspect before acting.
demos.payoff: One approved inspection, one recorded work order
demos.next: Where should your agents wait for a person?
demos.intro: One pump pressure reading has fallen after maintenance, while the other readings look normal. Fibey is an AI assistant helping the team investigate. It may check inventory, but a shift lead must approve an inspection work order. Orka will hold that action for a decision. The incident and work-order service in this demo are simulated.

chapters.title: Read the incident before acting
chapters.cue: Conflicting readings call for investigation
chapters.text: The pressure transmitter was replaced during maintenance. One reading then fell, while another gauge, flow, current, and vibration stayed normal. The request is to check inventory and propose an inspection. These facts support further investigation. They do not establish a diagnosis or authorize equipment changes.

chapters.title: Set the approval requirement
chapters.cue: Inventory is allowed; creating a work order requires approval
chapters.text: A Tool is an action Fibey can ask Orka to carry out. The saved policy allows an inventory lookup and a work-order request, but marks the work order as requiring approval. We also check the service's starting count. No work orders have been created for this run.

chapters.title: Start one Task for the investigation
chapters.cue: Task = the request and its continuing work record
chapters.text: A Task is Orka's record of this request. We create it and wait for an approval request. The same Task will connect the investigation, the pause for a decision, and the result returned to Fibey after the action runs.

chapters.title: Inspect exactly what is waiting
chapters.cue: Pending approval; execution has not started
chapters.text: The approval record names the requested tool and shows the stored action details. It identifies pump one and asks to inspect the pressure transmitter. Status is pending, and execution is not started. This is a concrete proposed action for the shift lead to review.

chapters.marker: 5. Check that work is still waiting
chapters.title: Verify the action has not run
chapters.cue: One inventory read; zero work orders before the decision
chapters.text: The service has received one inventory lookup and zero work orders. That is evidence from the receiving service, alongside Orka's pending record. Fibey has gathered information and proposed the next action, but the action is still waiting for a person's decision.

chapters.title: Approve the stored inspection request
chapters.cue: The decision records who approved and why
chapters.text: The presenter acts as the shift lead and approves this inspection request, with a reason that permits inspection and no equipment changes. Orka records the decision and the authenticated reviewer. It can now execute the stored action and return that action's result to the waiting Task.

chapters.marker: 7. Read the receipt and Fibey's answer
chapters.title: Check the receipt and continued answer
chapters.cue: Exactly one simulated work order after approval
chapters.text: The final evidence shows one completed inventory lookup, zero work orders before approval, and exactly one afterward. The original Task and tool call are retained. Fibey receives the actual work-order receipt and includes it in its answer. Its response also makes clear that the equipment has not been repaired yet.

demos.outro: Fibey investigated and prepared an inspection. A person approved the action, and its receipt came back to the same waiting Task. Where should your agents pause for a decision? Visit the Orka documentation at the address on screen to explore human approval and follow the getting started guide.
